documents.unit: Office of Community Standards / Board on Conduct Affairs
documents.title: Generative AI Policy Guidance
documents.summary: Stanford's Board on Conduct Affairs, adopted in February 2023, says that unless an instructor states otherwise, generative AI use is treated like help from another person and may not be used to substantially complete assignments or exams. Instructors may set their own rules, should put them in the syllabus, and may warn students about detection software. Students should acknowledge AI use and ask when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The document gives a fallback ("treated analogously to assistance from another person") but says "Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies ... allowing or disallowing some or all uses", so the decision is handed to instructors and the document is coded delegates, not restrict.

units.why: The passage states the purpose of the guidance: "set clear guidelines to students about what uses are and are not consistent with the Stanford Honor Code". It is an institution-level statement of purpose and scope, so P56 (framework/preamble), not a rule for any one course.
units.anchor: set clear guidelines to students about what uses are and are not consistent
units.frag_end: consistent with the Stanford Honor Code

units.why: The sentence "these tools can also be used in ways that bypass key learning objectives" gives the reason AI limits are needed: some uses skip the learning. P41 is nearest (AI shortcuts what builds skill), but it speaks of learning objectives rather than practice, hence a fit note.
units.anchor: these tools can also be used in ways that bypass key learning objectives
units.fit_note: Frames the concern as bypassing learning objectives, not explicitly as lost practice or skill-building. Coder A adds: says AI can bypass learning objectives; does not say that doing the work yourself builds skill.

units.why: "these tools have applications that foster student learning and understanding" names a benefit of AI without stating a rule or a career claim, which is P87 and not P44.
units.anchor: these tools have applications that foster student learning and understanding

units.why: The passage lists "ChatGPT, Bard, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion" as the tools covered. It defines the scope of the guidance by example, which is P61.
units.anchor: generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion
units.fit_note: Scope is defined only by named examples, including image generators, not by a formal definition.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. The source names "ChatGPT, Bard, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion" as the tools the guidance addresses, which is a statement of scope by example. Kept as a real scope statement (P61); the fit note records that no formal definition is given.

units.why: "Absent a clear statement from a course instructor" opens the fallback default for when the instructor says nothing, so P06 is the right type. The content of the fallback (analogy to another person) is coded separately as P45.
units.anchor: Absent a clear statement from a course instructor
units.policy: Absent a clear statement from a course instructor, use of or consultation with generative AI shall be treated analogously to assistance from another person.
units.fit_note: The fallback is not a ban: AI is treated like help from another person, which is allowed or not depending on Honor Code rules for such help.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded phase general and modality must; coder B coded course-start and informs. The source says "shall be treated analogously", a binding default, so modality is must. The default applies only when the instructor's syllabus statement is silent, so it is about communicating expectations: course-start. The content of the analogy is coded separately as P45.

units.why: "shall be treated analogously to assistance from another person" says AI is handled under the rules that govern help from a person. That is P45; the fallback framing of the same sentence is P06 above.
units.anchor: generative AI shall be treated analogously to assistance from another person

units.why: "using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam ... is not permitted" bans having AI produce the work submitted. P19 fits; it also names exams, but the core is producing the work, so not P22. The ban is limited to substantial completion.
units.anchor: using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam
units.frag_start: In particular, using generative AI tools
units.policy: Using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam is not permitted.
units.fit_note: Bans only substantial completion, not all use; also names exams. Coder A adds: also names entering exam or assignment questions as an example of the banned use, which overlaps P20 and P22.
units.resolution_why: Coder A folded the e.g. clause into this unit's policy; coder B split it into a separate P20 unit. Both agree on actor, phase, modality and type. The final keeps the clause as its own unit (P20) so each rule is coded once, and this unit states only the substantial-completion ban.

units.why: The parenthetical "e.g. by entering exam or assignment questions" gives a named example of prohibited use: putting questions into an AI tool. P20 (do not feed assignment specs to AI) matches.
units.anchor: by entering exam or assignment questions
units.policy: Entering exam or assignment questions into a generative AI tool is an example of using it to substantially complete an assignment or exam, which is not permitted.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this separately (A put it inside the P19 policy text). The parenthetical "e.g. by entering exam or assignment questions" names a distinct prohibited act, entering questions into an AI tool, matching P20. Kept as its own unit.

units.why: "Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI" asks for acknowledgment of AI use in submitted work, so P24; the modality is should, not must.
units.anchor: Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI
units.policy: Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI, other than incidental use.
units.fit_note: Excludes incidental use from the disclosure expectation (coder A's note; coded separately as P100).

units.why: "(other than incidental use)" exempts incidental use from acknowledgment, so minor AI use does not need disclosure. P100 (exempt routine features) is nearest; it does not name spell-check or similar features, hence the fit note.
units.policy: Incidental use of generative AI does not need to be acknowledged.
units.fit_note: Exempts 'incidental use' generally rather than named routine features such as spell-check.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this separately (A attached it to the P24 acknowledgment unit as a fit note). "(other than incidental use)" is a distinct exemption from the acknowledgment rule, so it stands as its own unit (P100); A's note is kept on the P24 unit.

units.why: "default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt" tells students to err toward disclosure when unsure. It is a disclosure rule (P24) with a doubt tiebreaker, which the type does not capture, so a fit note. P10 (ask before using) is about permission, not disclosure.
units.anchor: default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt
units.fit_note: Adds a tiebreaker: disclose when unsure whether acknowledgment is required.

units.why: "Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies ... including allowing or disallowing some or all uses" hands the decision to instructors, which is P04.
units.anchor: Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies regulating the use
units.frag_end: some or all uses of such tools.
units.policy: Individual course instructors are free to set their own policies regulating the use of generative AI tools in their courses, including allowing or disallowing some or all uses of such tools.

units.why: "Course instructors should set such policies in their course syllabi and clearly communicate such policies to students" tells instructors to put AI rules in the syllabus: P09.
units.anchor: Course instructors should set such policies in their course syllabi
units.policy: Course instructors should set their generative AI policies in their course syllabi and clearly communicate them to students.

units.why: "Students who are unsure of policies regarding generative AI tools are encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification" is the ask-when-unsure rule, P10.
units.anchor: Students who are unsure of policies regarding generative AI tools are encouraged to ask
units.frag_start: Students who are unsure of policies
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded phase during-work; coder B coded course-start. The sentence "Students who are unsure of policies ... are encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification" sits with the syllabus-communication guidance and concerns learning the course's expectations, not doing the work, so course-start.

units.why: "OCS recommends course instructors provide clear advance notice that they may use detection software" is about telling students that detectors may be used. It concerns detection tools (P40), but the unit is the advance-notice duty, so a fit note.
units.anchor: provide clear advance notice that they may use detection software
units.frag_start: As part of the BCA's guidance
units.frag_end: submitted for use of generative AI.
units.policy: OCS recommends that course instructors provide clear advance notice that they may use detection software to review submitted work for use of generative AI.
units.fit_note: Concerns advance notice to students that detection software may be used, not the use of the tool itself. Coder A: passage is about giving students advance notice that detection software may be used, not about how detection is used.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on actor, phase, modality and type but differed on unit_stance (A neutral, B permit). The passage only asks for advance notice; it takes no position on AI use, so neutral.

units.why: "The BCA will continue to monitor developments in these tools ... and may update this guidance" says the guidance is provisional and will be revisited: P54.
units.anchor: The BCA will continue to monitor developments in these tools
units.frag_start: The BCA will continue to monitor
units.policy: The BCA will continue to monitor developments in generative AI tools and their use in academic settings and may update this guidance.

units.why: "Members of the community are encouraged to contact the BCA to provide input, suggestions, and comments" invites feedback on the policy, which P54 covers ("feedback is invited").
units.anchor: encouraged to contact the BCA to provide input, suggestions, and comments
units.frag_start: Members of the community are encouraged

Only the Generative AI Policy Guidance section of the OCS page was coded; the rest of the saved page (hearing panels, proctoring, penalty code, enrollment holds) does not concern AI. The proctoring guidance bans remote proctoring but never mentions AI. The 'if you are in doubt ... talk with the instructor' line near the top repeats the later ask-the-instructor sentence and was coded once.
